title: Rick Atkinson speaks at UNH's Rutman Distinguished Lecture Series - The New Hampshire
content: On Tuesday, Oct. 20, the University of New Hampshire welcomed Pulitzer-prize winning journalist and historian, Rick Atkinson to speak for this year's Rutman Lecture Series in the Memorial Union Building (MUB). The Rutman Lecture Series began in 2013 and has since invited academics to speak on American Presidencies, Atkinson chose to analyze the first and most famous president, George Washington. Specifically, Atkinson looked at Washington through the lens of war using his knowledge from writing eight narrative history books about five wars including the American Revolution. “Where does a writer begin writing about George Washington?” Said Atkinson. Atkinson and other historians have the unique challenge of describing events with details that are found purely through research. Atkinson found many characteristics of Washington that are commonly overlooked, describing him as opaque, molten tempered and pitiful of himself. Washington was not the best general either, and when he was promoted to commander in chief, he read what Atkinson described as a “war for dummies” handbook due to his lack of experience. A question Atkinson explored in his lecture was, If Washington was not fit for the role of commander in chief and had unpleasant characteristics, why has he been put on such a pedestal by Americans? Atkinson explained that Washington had a higher calling as a leader. “Washington has the ability to rise to the occasion,” said Atkinson. Washington had instincts to know the most optimal way to influence and compromise as a leader. On another note, Atkinson described Washington as physically robust considering he never caught a cold during the war. It also helped that Washington was six-foot-two in a time when the average height of a man was five feet eight inches, giving him further physical advantages. Washington’s character was not the only thing overlooked by many Americans, the Revolutionary War itself was relentlessly violent on all sides of combat, as Atkinson described. The American side had many flaws itself. The rebel government in Pennsylvania would execute anyone suspected of being a traitor or loyal to the British. Atkinson highlighted that the Americans were truly relentless in their battle, even when faced with many cities burning and falling. “Even a profounding British triumph would not have been enough”, said Atkinson. Atkinson has written about war time and time again because it “shapes our history.” It has been prevalent in our history nationally and globally. Atkinson informed the audience that only 268 years have been without war out of over three thousand years of recorded human history. “Unfortunately none of those 268 years have any of us been alive,” said Atkinson. Valerie Reynolds is a junior English/Journalism and Justice Studies student at UNH. Additionally, she is Political Editor of The New Hampshire. Valerie has been with TNH for 2 years. She strives to achieve ethical, honest and informative journalism and has reported stories of her own on government, AI, enforcement, and more. Beyond her academic work, she enjoys staying active by taking dance classes and working out.

title: Leaner and Meaner: Are UNH's Profits Getting Bigger? Buy Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH is becoming more profitable while serving fewer members. Third-quarter results suggest that Optum's turnaround efforts and UnitedHealthcare's pricing discipline are restoring margins, even as revenues and enrollment face pressure. However, sustaining this recovery will require continued execution, tight medical-cost management and an ability to navigate a changing political landscape. Is UNH positioned for lasting earnings growth? Optum leads that shift. Its operating earnings increased to $3.73 billion from $2.51 billion, as revenues declined to $66.9 billion from $69.2 billion. At Optum Health, operating profit rose to $735 million from just $41 million. Its margin reached 3.2% compared with a 0.2% margin a year earlier. Discipline is returning, although margin remains well below management's target of 6-8% by 2028. Optum Health's revenues declined 10% to $22.9 billion as the company withdrew from markets where its value-based care presence lacked sufficient scale. While the retreat helps eliminate underperforming arrangements, sustained profitability will depend on expanding patient relationships within established markets. Optum Health currently serves about 20 million patients, including roughly 4 million in fully accountable care arrangements, leaving room to deepen its integrated care model. Growth opportunities include home health, surgery centers and complex-care management, where earlier intervention could reduce costly hospitalizations. Home health visits increased 10% in the quarter, while online self-scheduling rose 27%, indicating progress in patient access. The challenge now is converting these operational improvements into sustainable revenue growth and higher margins. Two other Optum businesses provide an earnings cushion. Optum Insight's operating earnings reached $1.28 billion, up from $920 million, on revenue growth of about 3%. Operating margin jumped to 23.4% from 17.3% a year ago. Automation could lower claims-processing and documentation costs for customers. A new coding product has 15 live clients, with 24 more being implemented. Optum Rx is also finding ways to earn more from less volume. Operating earnings climbed to $1.72 billion from $1.55 billion, although adjusted prescriptions fell to 393 million from 414 million. Greater biosimilar adoption and operational improvements supported profitability. Specialty pharmacy volumes, meanwhile, increased 2.6%, even as overall scripts declined. More than half of Optum Rx membership now comes from outside UnitedHealthcare, reducing its reliance on its sister insurer. Transparent, fee-based pricing could strengthen customer retention as pharmacy benefit managers face demands for simpler drug economics. Its operating margin of 4.3% grew 40 bps from a year ago. UnitedHealthcare's numbers tell a similar story. Its operating earnings rose to $2.83 billion from $1.81 billion, despite revenues easing to $86.3 billion from $87.1 billion. The operating margin improved to 3.3% from 2.1%. At the group level, the medical care ratio dropped to 88.4% from 89.9%, while the operating cost ratio fell to 12.8% from 13.5%. Better pricing, benefit design and claims management are helping the insurer keep more of each premium dollar. However, the medical care ratio benefited from $610 million of favorable reserve development related to earlier 2026 service periods. UnitedHealthcare enters 2027 with a narrower, potentially healthier book of business. Medical membership fell to 48.3 million from 50.1 million a year ago, reflecting deliberate Medicare Advantage repositioning and other losses. Growth is shifting toward special needs plans. UNH is concentrating on high-value HMOs and plans serving people with chronic conditions or dual eligibility, where coordinated care can support both outcomes and economics. The Democrats' victory in the midterm elections could reshape the healthcare industry's policy outlook. Set to control both chambers of Congress from January 2027, Democrats may push to reverse Medicaid funding cuts and restore subsidies. Such measures could support insurance enrollment and ease funding pressures on healthcare providers. However, the benefits may vary across insurers. Medicaid-focused players like Molina Healthcare, Inc. MOH and Centene Corporation CNC could gain more directly than UnitedHealth, given UNH's substantial Medicare Advantage exposure. Meanwhile, increased congressional oversight of Medicare Advantage practices, prior authorizations and pharmacy benefit managers could create fresh challenges for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Rx. President Trump's veto power and legislative hurdles could delay major policy changes. For UNH, the election introduces potential funding relief but also regulatory uncertainty, making execution and policy developments important determinants of its recovery. Looking at the year-to-date period, UNH stock has gained 19.4%, outperforming the S&P 500’s 7.2% rise, but trailing the industry’s 22.9% growth. Peers like Molina Healthcareand Centenehave increased 20.5% and 69.5%, respectively, during this time. Commercial medical-cost trends continue to exceed UNH's expectations, driven partly by costly specialty drugs and payment disputes under the No Surprises Act. Although pricing adjustments and operational improvements are supporting margins, shrinking insurance membership and lower Optum Health revenues leave less room for execution errors. Medicaid reimbursement rates have also struggled to keep pace with patient acuity, with management expecting core Medicaid margins to remain moderately better than negative 1% in 2026. Persistent funding mismatches could delay profitability improvements, particularly if medical utilization remains elevated. Profit growth appears achievable if medical-cost pressures remain manageable. Management raised its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to at least $20.50 and considers the lower end of its long-term 13-16% growth target a reasonable starting point for 2027. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 EPS stands at $20.61, indicating 26.1% year-over-year growth, while revenues are projected at $449.11 billion, up 0.4%. For 2027, EPS is expected to rise 13.4% to $23.38, alongside 3.2% revenue growth to $463.41 billion. Estimate revisions reinforce the positive outlook, with 14 upward EPS revisions for 2026 and 13 for 2027 over the past month, against no cuts. The company beat earnings estimates in each of the past four quarters, producing an average earnings surprise of 14%. Despite the stock’s ytd rise, the average analyst price target of $475.96 suggests an upside of 20.3% from current levels. UnitedHealth's recovery is gaining traction, with improved insurance margins, Optum's operational turnaround and greater cost discipline supporting profitability despite a smaller membership base. The company's focus on higher-value care arrangements and profitable growth provides a foundation for sustained earnings improvement, although elevated medical costs and reimbursement pressures remain challenges. Encouraging earnings estimate revisions, management's constructive 2027 outlook and a valuation below historical levels strengthen the investment case. Entering overtime, the UMass Lowell hockey team had momentum and 57 seconds of a power play. But the River Hawks couldn’t mount any pressure, took a penalty of their own and then watched as New Hampshire’s Emile Guite scored a 3-on-3 goal to lift the Wildcats to a 5-4 Hockey East victory over the River Hawks on Saturday at the Whittemore Center in Durham, N.H. UML lost the draw, Guite lifted the stick of a River Hawks player and sent a shot past Austin Elliott for the winning goal. “Nobody is ever content in a loss but tonight the compete was there,” said UML head coach Norm Bazin. “Several new players came into the lineup, which gave our team a different look. We kept fighting back all game despite some questionable calls. We showed some heart tying the game late and I thought we got back to Lowell-style hockey. We need to learn from this overtime experience but I do believe we deserved a better fate today. We focus on our preparation for two non-conference opponents this week.” The River Hawks (2-8, 0-4 HE) earned their first Hockey East point, but the Wildcats took five of six points from UML this weekend. Junior Jacob MacDonald had a career-high three-assist performance for UML, which tied the game 4-4 with 1:29 remaining after the River Hawks pulled Elliott for a sixth skater. UNH outshot UML 39-17, forcing Elliott to make 34 saves. Freshman Misha Volotovskii scored his second collegiate goal for UML to tie the game at 12:45 of the third. The goal stood after a lengthy video review. But UNH’s Nick Ring tallied his fifth goal of the season at 16:29. Sophomore Cole Lonsdale lifted the River Hawks into a 1-0 lead just 1:18 into the game. Lonsdale (No. 2 of season) scored on his own rebound after he was set up by MacDonald. Defenseman Sean Kilcullen also assisted on the play. But the Wildcats evened it 12 minutes later as Ryan Philbrick sent a shot past Elliott. Nick VanTassell gave UNH a 2-1 lead in the second period before the teams traded power play goals. UML sophomore Dalyn Wakely (No. 2) slapped home the rebound of a MacDonald shot for a man advantage strike at the 13:17 mark. title: UNH football rallies in final minute to beat Rhode Island - Yahoo Sports
content: DURHAM — Sophomore quarterback Tommy McLeish threw for two touchdowns and caught another to lift the University of New Hampshire football team to a 24-21 victory over the University of Rhode Island on Saturday at Wildcat Stadium. With UNH trailing 21-17 and 1:53 remaining, McLeish engineered an 11-play, 64-yard drive capped by a 1-yard touchdown pass to tight end Colby Ramshaw with 7 seconds remaining, giving the Wildcats a 24-21 lead. McLeish completed 21 of 37 passes for 271 yards and two touchdowns. He also caught a 7-yard touchdown pass from sophomore wide receiver Ryan Ricketti. Junior wide receiver Logan Perez caught four passes for 91 yards, including a 52-yard touchdown, while senior wide receiver Ja'Carree Kelly had five catches for 91 yards. Graduate student running back Myles Thomason rushed for a team-high 84 yards on 16 carries. Sophomore linebacker Trevor Barry, who entered the game leading the FCS in tackles per game, finished with 10 tackles. Graduate student safety Jackson Stone added nine tackles and an interception. Rhode Island was led by Brayden Richardson, who rushed for a game-high 138 yards, including a 64-yard touchdown. Alex McClelland completed 10 of 24 passes for 142 yards and a touchdown and added 50 rushing yards on 17 carries. New Hampshire returns to action Saturday, Nov. 14 at 1 p.m. against Stony Brook University.
